title: A SEXUAL CRIME INSIDE DAVID’S HOUSE BECAME THE SPARK FOR MURDER AND FAMILY WAR—AND THE SILENCE OF A FATHER HELPED DESTROY HIS OWN FAMILY
paragraphs: A SEXUAL CRIME INSIDE DAVID’S HOUSE BECAME THE SPARK FOR MURDER AND FAMILY WAR—AND THE SILENCE OF A FATHER HELPED DESTROY HIS OWN FAMILY

She was a king’s daughter. He was her own brother. She begged him to stop. But what happened behind that locked door would expose a terrifying truth: when sin is protected, victims are silenced, and justice is delayed, an entire family can bleed from a wound nobody was willing to confront. The tragedy of 2 Samuel 13 is not just about what Amnon did to Tamar. It is about what happened when everyone else had a chance to respond.
There are some Bible stories that make you want to close the book.
Not because they are difficult to understand.
But because you understand them too well.
Because somewhere in the story, you recognize a family you know.
A daughter who stopped smiling.
A father who knew something terrible had happened but never seemed to do enough.
A brother whose anger became something dangerous.
A household where everybody knew something was wrong, but nobody wanted to talk about it.
And perhaps the most painful part?
The person who caused the damage kept living as though the wounded person was the problem.
This is one of those stories.
And before we walk through it, I need you to understand something.

The Bible does not tell us about Tamar to entertain us with scandal. It tells the truth about a crime committed against her, refusing to pretend that royal blood, religious identity, or family reputation can make evil less evil.

If you have ever been hurt by someone who was supposed to protect you, this passage may be painful. You do not have to force yourself through every detail. And if this story resembles something that happened to you, hear this clearly: the wrong committed against Tamar was not her fault. The wrong committed against you was not made righteous by someone else's authority, reputation, or position in the family.
Now come with me into the house of David.
Not onto the battlefield where he defeated Goliath.
Not into the wilderness where he wrote songs of trust.
But into his own home.
Because sometimes the place where people expect to be safest becomes the place where their deepest wounds begin.
And what happened in that house would eventually leave a daughter devastated, a son murdered, another son fleeing, and a kingdom moving toward rebellion.
The story begins with a sentence that should make every reader uncomfortable.
Amnon, one of David's sons, became obsessed with Tamar, the beautiful sister of Absalom and Amnon's half-sister.
Scripture says Amnon was so distressed over Tamar that he became sick.
At first glance, someone might mistake his obsession for love.
But the Bible is about to expose the difference between love and lust.
Love protects.
Lust takes.
Love considers the dignity of another person.
Lust asks only how to satisfy itself.
And when a desire becomes more important than another person's dignity, safety, and freedom, it has already begun to reveal the darkness inside the human heart.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, described as a very shrewd man.
Instead of confronting Amnon's sinful desire, Jonadab suggested a plan.
Pretend to be sick.
Ask the king to send Tamar to prepare food.
Arrange to be alone with her.
Think about that.
An evil desire found an accomplice in cleverness.
The plan did not require an army.
It required deception, access, and the trust of a family.
David, apparently unaware of the scheme, sent Tamar to Amnon.
And Tamar went.
Why wouldn't she?
Her father had instructed her to care for her brother.
She was doing something good.
Something compassionate.
Something ordinary.
And that ordinary act of kindness was exploited by someone determined to do evil.
There is a painful lesson here.
Being obedient, kind, trusting, or compassionate does not make a person responsible when someone else chooses to abuse that trust.
Tamar did not cause Amnon's crime by entering his room.
Amnon was responsible for what he chose to do.
When she prepared the food, Amnon refused to eat.
He ordered everyone else out.
Then he called Tamar closer.
And suddenly, what had appeared to be an innocent request became a trap.
He seized her and demanded that she lie with him.
Tamar resisted.
Her words are among the most heartbreaking in this entire chapter.
In 2 Samuel 13:12, the Hebrew text begins:
אַל־אָחִי אַל־תְּעַנֵּנִי
ʾAl-ʾāḥî, ʾal-teʿannēnî.
The sense is:
“No, my brother, do not violate me.”
Notice what she calls him.
My brother.
Two words that should have reminded him of a relationship that required protection and restraint.
She was appealing to the very bond he was betraying.
The Hebrew verb translated here as “violate” carries the sense of humiliating or afflicting someone. In this context, Tamar is explicitly resisting sexual violence.
She continues by identifying the act as something that must not be done in Israel.
She does not speak as someone consenting.
She does not welcome his demand.
She resists it.
She reasons with him.
She appeals to morality.
She pleads.
And he refuses to listen.
That refusal matters.
Because sometimes people read ancient stories and overlook what the text makes painfully clear.
Tamar said no.
And Amnon ignored her.
In 2 Samuel 13:14, the Hebrew says:
וְלֹא אָבָה לִשְׁמֹעַ בְּקוֹלָהּ
Ve-lōʾ ʾāvāh lishmōaʿ be-qōlāh.
“But he would not listen to her voice.”
Then Scripture records that he overpowered and violated her.
The text does not celebrate this act.
It exposes it.
And it matters deeply that the Bible preserves Tamar's voice.
Her protest is not erased from the sacred record.
Her refusal is not treated as irrelevant.
Her suffering is not rewritten as romance.
The narrator places responsibility on the man who would not listen.
There is something every Christian household, church, ministry, and community must understand.
A person's authority does not give them ownership of another person's body.
Being family does not make sexual violence less serious.
Being respected does not make an abuser innocent.
Being religious does not make wrongdoing holy.
And forgiveness must never be used as an excuse to conceal abuse, deny justice, or pressure victims into unsafe relationships.
Amnon had the status of a prince.
But his status did not make his actions righteous.
Then something happened that revealed how utterly false his supposed love had been.
After violating Tamar, Amnon began to hate her.
Scripture says his hatred became greater than the love he had claimed to feel.
He ordered her to leave.
Imagine the cruelty.
He had already taken what she had refused to give.
Now he wanted her removed from his sight.
Tamar protested again, recognizing the further wrong of casting her away.
But he would not listen.
Again.
He called a servant and had her put outside.
The door was shut behind her.
And there she stood.
A daughter of the king.
Wounded.
Rejected.
Cast out of the very room where her trust had been betrayed.
She tore the special robe associated with the unmarried daughters of the king.
She put ashes on her head.
She placed her hand upon her head and went away crying aloud.
The Hebrew describes her as:
הָלוֹךְ וְזָעָקָה
Hālôkh ve-zāʿāqāh.
The expression portrays her going along and crying out.
She was not quietly pretending nothing had happened.
Her grief was visible.
Her anguish was audible.
And I wonder how many people reading this know what it feels like to carry a wound while everyone around them wants life to continue as normal.
Perhaps nobody assaulted you.
Perhaps your wound came through betrayal, manipulation, abandonment, humiliation, or a trusted person's cruelty.
The circumstances are different, and they should not all be treated as equivalent.
But you may recognize the loneliness of suffering while others seem more concerned about keeping the peace than confronting the truth.
Tamar's brother Absalom discovered what had happened.
He told her to remain quiet and took her into his house.
The biblical account says Tamar lived there desolate.
That word deserves attention.
In 2 Samuel 13:20, the Hebrew describes her condition using the word:
שֹׁמֵמָה
Shōmēmāh.
It conveys devastation or desolation.
A life marked by what had happened.
A woman whose future had been profoundly disrupted by another person's sin.
And this is where we must resist a dangerous misunderstanding.
Tamar was not morally ruined by being assaulted.
Her dignity before God did not disappear.
Her value was not reduced.
Her suffering was real, but the guilt belonged to the one who violated her.
The world may have treated her as disgraced.
Scripture does not require us to agree with that judgment.
In fact, the Bible's wider testimony gives us reason to reject it.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that human beings are created in God's image.
That image is not erased by another person's violence.
A victim does not become less human, less worthy of care, or less loved by God because of someone else's crime.
And now the story moves toward another terrible moment.
David hears what happened.
Second Samuel 13:21 says he became very angry.
Angry.
But the chapter does not record him bringing Amnon to justice.
It does not describe David publicly defending Tamar.
It does not tell us that he took decisive action to restrain his son.
We should not invent conversations or actions the text does not reveal.
But we cannot ignore what the narrative does show.
David's anger did not prevent the violence that followed.
And his failure to address the situation decisively stands in painful contrast to the authority he possessed as king and father.
A king who could command armies could not undo his daughter's suffering.
But he could have acted against wrongdoing.
And the absence of recorded justice becomes part of the tragedy.
This is where the story stops feeling ancient.
Because some families have mastered the art of being angry without being accountable.
They are furious when wrongdoing becomes public.
They are embarrassed when someone speaks.
They are distressed when the family name is threatened.
But the person who was hurt is still waiting for someone to do what is right.
A father may say, “I am disappointed.”
A leader may say, “We are praying about it.”
A relative may say, “We don't want to divide the family.”
But when those words become substitutes for protection, truth, and accountability, they can leave the vulnerable exposed.
Anger is not the same as justice.
Regret is not the same as repentance.
And silence is not the same as peace.
Now consider Absalom.
He knew what had happened to his sister.
He hated Amnon.
But for two years he said neither good nor bad to him.
Two years.
Two years of unresolved hatred.
Two years of living with a wound in the family.
Two years in which the narrative gives us no account of reconciliation or justice.
Then Absalom arranged a sheep-shearing celebration.
He invited the king's sons.
And he specifically sought to have Amnon present.
David initially declined to attend himself but eventually permitted Amnon and the other sons to go.
Absalom instructed his servants to wait until Amnon had been drinking wine and then kill him at his command.
They did.
The prince who had violated Tamar was murdered by the servants of her brother.
But this was not the restoration of Tamar.
It was another grave wrong.
And we need to say that carefully.
Absalom's anger at the crime against his sister is understandable.
His decision to arrange a murder was not righteous.
Scripture does not give victims or their families a license for private revenge.
Romans 12:19 calls believers to leave vengeance to God.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the responsibility of governing authorities to restrain wrongdoing.
Biblical justice is not indifference.
But neither is it personal retaliation disguised as holiness.
Absalom did not heal the household.
He added bloodshed to its suffering.
When the news first reached David, the report was even worse than what had happened.
He was told that Absalom had killed all the king's sons.
David tore his garments and lay on the ground.
Later, it became clear that Amnon alone had been killed.
The other sons returned.
And the royal household wept.
Imagine the sound of that house.
A daughter had cried because her brother violated her.
Now a father cried because another son had been murdered.
A brother had become a killer.
A family was breaking apart.
And Absalom fled to Geshur, where he remained for three years.
The story in 2 Samuel 13 ends with grief, separation, and unfinished conflict.
It does not end with everyone gathered around a table.
It does not end with a beautiful apology.
It does not tell us that Tamar received the justice, protection, or restoration she deserved.
That unresolved ending should trouble us.
Because Scripture is not obligated to give every tragedy a comfortable conclusion.
Sometimes it leaves the wound visible so we will not pretend the wound was small.
And the consequences did not stop there.
The following chapters show Absalom returning, growing estranged from David, and eventually leading a rebellion against his father.
Second Samuel 15–18 records the devastating conflict that followed.
We should not reduce every later event to one single cause. Absalom made his own choices, and the narrative includes political ambition, resentment, estrangement, and other factors.
But the sexual violence against Tamar, the murder of Amnon, and the fractured relationships within David's family form an essential part of the story's tragic progression.
And behind this family catastrophe stands an even larger biblical context.
Earlier, in 2 Samuel 11, David himself had taken Bathsheba and arranged for Uriah's death.
The account of David and Bathsheba includes a profound abuse of royal power, and the text does not give us grounds to assume an equal, freely chosen relationship.
When the prophet Nathan confronted David in 2 Samuel 12, he declared that the sword would not depart from David's house.
The Hebrew warning includes the words:
לֹא־תָסוּר חֶרֶב מִבֵּיתְךָ
Lōʾ-tāsûr ḥerev mib-bêtekha.
“The sword shall never depart from your house.”
The warning was not permission for David's children to sin.
Nor does it mean Tamar deserved what happened to her.
She did not.
Rather, the unfolding narrative reveals the terrible consequences surrounding David's sin and the destructive choices made within his household.
David's repentance was real.
Psalm 51 gives voice to his plea for mercy, and 2 Samuel 12:13 records Nathan telling him that the Lord had put away his sin.
Yet forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
This is a truth modern Christianity sometimes struggles to hold together.
God truly forgives repentant sinners.
And sinful actions can still leave devastating consequences.
Grace is not denial.
Mercy is not the cancellation of truth.
Forgiveness is not a command to erase evidence, abandon accountability, or restore access to someone who remains dangerous.
The Gospel never requires us to call evil good.
And now I want to speak to the person who has been carrying a secret for years.
Maybe your family told you to stay quiet.
Maybe the person who hurt you was respected.
Maybe everyone believed the person with the better reputation.
Maybe you prayed for the pain to disappear, but it kept returning in the middle of ordinary days.
Perhaps you began wondering whether God saw any of it.
Tamar's story cannot answer every question about your circumstances.
But it does reveal something important about the God who gave us Scripture.
He did not allow this terrible crime to be completely erased from the biblical record.
He preserved Tamar's protest.
He preserved the account of her suffering.
He allowed generations of readers to hear what Amnon refused to hear.
Her voice.
And when we turn to Jesus Christ, we encounter a Savior who did not treat wounded people as disposable.
In Luke 4:18, Jesus announced good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed as He read from Isaiah.
In Matthew 11:28, He invited the weary and burdened to come to Him.
In John 8, He exposed the hypocrisy of those eager to condemn another person while refusing to examine themselves.
And in the Gospels, again and again, He moved toward people others had pushed aside.
This does not mean every wounded person will receive immediate healing.
It does not mean faith removes the need for counseling, safety, medical care, or legal protection.
It means the suffering person is not beneath the attention of Christ.
He sees people whom others overlook.
He does not need us to pretend that something was harmless when it was devastating.
And He never asks us to build His kingdom by protecting evil.
But perhaps you are reading this story from a different place.
Perhaps you recognize something of Amnon's selfishness.
Not necessarily his specific crime, but the frightening capacity of the human heart to want something so badly that it begins justifying wrongdoing.
Perhaps you have manipulated someone.
Perhaps you have treated another person's trust as an opportunity.
Perhaps you have hidden behind excuses.
Then hear this.
Do not confuse conviction with condemnation that leaves you hopeless.
The purpose of genuine conviction is to bring sin into the light and turn the sinner toward repentance.
But repentance is more than feeling ashamed.
It means turning away from evil.
It means abandoning excuses.
It means telling the truth.
It means accepting appropriate consequences.
And when harm has been committed, it means refusing to demand forgiveness, reconciliation, or access to the person who was hurt.
The blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse repentant sinners.
First John 1:9 tells us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
But confession is not a loophole around accountability.
A person cannot claim to honor Christ while insisting that the wounded remain silent to preserve the offender's comfort.
Real repentance bears fruit.
And sometimes the fruit of repentance includes accepting boundaries, making restitution where possible, cooperating with lawful authorities, and surrendering the right to control how others respond.
Then there is David.
The father who became angry.
The man who knew what it meant to sin grievously and need mercy.
The king whose household was collapsing.
Perhaps this is where some parents, pastors, and spiritual leaders need to examine themselves.
What happens when protecting a reputation becomes more important than protecting a person?
What happens when we are so afraid of scandal that we neglect justice?
What happens when we preach forgiveness to the wounded before we have confronted the wrongdoing?
What happens when the person who speaks up is treated as the threat to unity?
A family can look peaceful in photographs while someone inside it is suffering.
A church can sing beautifully while someone in its congregation is afraid to tell the truth.
A ministry can have influence, resources, and public respect while still failing to care for the vulnerable.
None of those outward appearances can replace righteousness.
Micah 6:8 calls God's people to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with Him.
James 1:27 speaks of caring for the vulnerable and remaining unstained by the world.
Ephesians 5:11 instructs believers not to participate in works of darkness but to expose them.
These passages do not mean allegations should be handled carelessly or that due process is unimportant.
Truth matters for everyone involved.
But they do mean that the pursuit of truth, protection, and justice cannot be sacrificed simply because the facts may be embarrassing.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a comforting religious phrase.
Because if the story ended with David's family, we would be left staring at the wreckage.
A wounded daughter.
A murdered son.
A fugitive brother.
A grieving father.
And the painful realization that even the household of Israel's celebrated king was not immune to terrible evil.
But the Bible does not end with David.
It leads us to the Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
The King who did not come to exploit those beneath Him.
The King who came to serve.
The King who had authority but did not use that authority for selfish gratification.
The King who confronted hypocrisy, showed compassion to the vulnerable, and gave His life for sinners.
David was an imperfect king who needed forgiveness.
Jesus is the sinless King who provides redemption.
And that contrast matters.
Because Christianity is not ultimately built upon the moral perfection of David.
It is built upon the person and saving work of Jesus Christ.
David's family reveals the terrible damage sin can cause.
Christ reveals God's answer to sin at its deepest level.
At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment due to sinners.
He did not dismiss evil as insignificant.
He did not declare that wrongdoing had never mattered.
He gave Himself as the atoning sacrifice through whom forgiveness and reconciliation with God become possible.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin, death, and the grave would not have the final word.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a message about becoming nicer people.
It is the announcement that God saves sinners through the death and resurrection of His Son.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone who is in Christ is a new creation.
But new creation does not mean pretending the past never happened.
It means the past no longer has ultimate authority to define what God can make of a person in Christ.
For the wounded, this means the wrong done to you does not determine your worth.
For the repentant sinner, this means the mercy of God offers a real path away from the old life.
For the person who has remained silent in the face of wrongdoing, this means it is not too late to begin choosing truth and righteousness.
And for those who are still waiting for justice, it means that the final judgment belongs to a God who is neither deceived nor indifferent.
Revelation 21:4 points toward a day when God will wipe away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise does not tell us to ignore suffering today.
It gives us hope while we seek what is right today.
Some wounds require years of patient care.
Some relationships cannot safely be restored.
Some wrongs must be reported to the proper authorities.
Some consequences remain even after sincere repentance.
And some questions may remain unanswered in this life.
Yet Christ is not absent from those difficult realities.
He is not honored when we rush wounded people into pretending they are healed.
He is honored when we speak truthfully, love faithfully, protect the vulnerable, and refuse to use His name as a cover for evil.

If you are in danger, seek safety and appropriate help. If someone has disclosed abuse to you, listen carefully, take their safety seriously, and involve qualified professionals or relevant authorities as appropriate. Prayer and practical protection belong together.
And if you have been wondering whether your life can still have meaning after what happened, please hear this.
Tamar's story is not proof that wounded people are beyond restoration.
It is proof that the Bible is willing to tell the truth about wounds that human beings often try to hide.
We are not told everything that happened in Tamar's later life.
We should not invent a happy ending for her simply to make ourselves feel better.
But neither should we allow the last detail recorded about her to become a declaration that every wounded person's future must remain desolate.
Jesus Christ offers hope that reaches beyond the worst chapter of a human life.
Not always by changing everything overnight.
Not by requiring silence.
Not by erasing memory.
But by bringing His presence, truth, mercy, and sustaining grace into places where human strength has failed.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this has needed for years.
What happened to you may have changed your life, but it did not change your value before God.
I wish I could sit beside every person reading this who has spent years believing otherwise.
The one who thinks their family would have been happier if they had never spoken.
The one who feels guilty because somebody else's wrongdoing destroyed the peace.
The one who has prayed for healing and still has difficult days.
The one who has been told to forgive but has never heard the words, “What happened to you was wrong.”
You deserve to hear the truth.
The responsibility belongs to the person who committed the wrong.
Your safety matters.
Your voice matters.
Your dignity matters.
And Jesus Christ is not ashamed to receive people who come to Him carrying grief, confusion, and wounds they cannot explain.
Perhaps you are not the wounded person in this story.
Perhaps you are the friend who has been afraid to get involved.
The relative who suspected something.
The leader who kept postponing a difficult conversation.
The parent who thought silence would keep the family together.
Then let the story of David's house confront you.
Because silence may look peaceful for a season while the consequences of unaddressed evil continue growing.
Not every silence is sinful; victims have the right to privacy and control over their own disclosures. But those responsible for protecting others must not use silence as an excuse for inaction.
The call is not to spread rumors.
The call is to act with truth, wisdom, courage, and care.
And if this passage has uncovered something in your own heart, do not hurry past it.
Maybe you need to repent.
Maybe you need to ask forgiveness without demanding that someone give it.
Maybe you need to stop defending a person simply because they are related to you.
Maybe you need to seek help.
Maybe you need to believe, perhaps for the first time, that Christ receives the brokenhearted.
Or maybe you need to admit that you have been carrying more pain than you have allowed anyone to see.
You can bring that truth to God.
You do not have to manufacture beautiful words.
You do not have to perform strength.
You can pray something as simple as:

“Lord Jesus, You know what happened. You know what I have done, what I have suffered, and what I have hidden. Lead me into truth. Teach me genuine repentance where I have sinned. Give me courage to seek help where I have been wounded. Protect those who are vulnerable. Heal what can be healed. Help me trust Your goodness without denying the reality of evil. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
What part of this story stayed with you the most?
Was it Tamar begging to be heard?
Was it Amnon refusing to listen?
Was it David's anger without the decisive justice the story leaves us longing to see?
Was it Absalom allowing hatred to become murder?
Or was it the realization that Jesus is a better King than every human leader who has ever failed us?
You can write, “Lord, teach me to stand for truth.”
If you have experienced abuse, please do not feel pressured to disclose your experience publicly. You owe no one your story. Your privacy and safety are more important than a comment.
And if this message has reminded you that God is still working in your life, you can write, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your words may help another reader realize that they are not alone.
This is also a message worth sharing beyond this page.
Someone may need to understand that biblical forgiveness does not excuse abuse.
Someone may need to hear that genuine repentance requires truth.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus Christ receives people who feel forgotten.
Not because it contains an easy answer to every painful situation, but because the truths in 2 Samuel 13 deserve to be remembered long after the emotion of reading has passed.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow as well.
We want to keep opening the Bible honestly.
Not avoiding difficult passages.
Not turning tragedy into entertainment.
Not preaching a version of Christianity that protects appearances while neglecting people.
But proclaiming Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel.
And if this ministry has been spiritually meaningful to you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something anyone can purchase.
But the Bible also teaches that believers may freely and generously support faithful Gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers partnering financially in Gospel work.
And 1 Corinthians 9:14 recognizes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support through that ministry.
That is the biblical spirit in which we invite you.
But it can be a meaningful act of stewardship.
A practical way of saying, “I want sound biblical teaching, encouragement, and the message of Jesus Christ to keep reaching people.”
It can help us continue bringing difficult Scriptures into the light with reverence, compassion, and biblical faithfulness.
And it can help us make more discipleship material accessible to people who may not have the resources to purchase books or Bible study tools.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, prayer, spiritual maturity, and their walk with Jesus Christ.
The library is free because we believe access to biblical nourishment should not depend on someone's ability to pay.
And voluntary support helps make work like this more sustainable.
It is the opportunity to participate in a ministry that wants to keep pointing people to Christ.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep sharing Scripture.
Keep praying for this ministry.
There are many ways to serve the Gospel faithfully.
What matters is not the size of a payment.
What matters is a heart surrendered to Christ.
Because the message of Gospel Warrior is not that money rewrites lives.
It is that Jesus Christ rewrites lives.
Not by declaring evil harmless.
Not by pretending consequences disappear.
Not by requiring victims to hide their wounds.
But through truth, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
David's household reminds us that sin can devastate even the most prominent family.
Tamar's suffering reminds us that the voices of the wounded must not be dismissed.
Amnon's crime reminds us how destructive unchecked desire can become.
Absalom's murder reminds us that revenge cannot become our substitute for justice.
David's failures remind us that even great spiritual figures desperately need the mercy of God.
And Jesus Christ reminds us that the failures of human kings are not the final measure of the goodness of our heavenly King.
So when you remember this story, do not remember only the scandal.
Remember the warning.
Remember the wounded.
Remember the call to truth.
Remember the need for repentance.
Remember the Savior who came into a world filled with real evil and gave His life to redeem sinners.
And remember that the Gospel offers hope without asking us to lie about what happened.
One day, every hidden thing will stand before the perfect justice of God.
And for those who belong to Christ, there is a promised future in which evil will not reign, tears will not endure forever, and death itself will be defeated.
Until then, may we be people who listen when Tamar cries.
People who refuse to protect wrongdoing.
People who seek justice without surrendering to vengeance.
People who offer grace without denying truth.
People who point the brokenhearted toward Jesus.
And people who never forget that the King who saves us is also the King who calls us to walk in the light.
The door they shut on Tamar could not shut her voice out of Scripture—and the wounds people try to bury are never hidden from the eyes of God.
